findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing with empty
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) only when the key is absent and ("", nil) when the key is present with an empty value (src/store.go:7-12). LoadOrDefault does `v, _ := Load(key, m)` and returns v, collapsing both cases to "". Any caller must treat an absent key as a real empty string: it cannot apply a distinct default, cannot error out, and cannot audit/validate a missing configuration value. Because the function is exported (package store), every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with a legitimate value; the unusable contract is itself the defect, not merely a risk to future callers.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing, conflating missing key with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) for an absent key and ("", nil) for a key that legitimately holds an empty string. LoadOrDefault (src/store.go:16) explicitly discards the error via `v, _ := Load(key, m)` and returns only a string, so every caller receives "" for both 'key missing' and 'key present with empty value' and can no longer distinguish failure from a real value. The error signal that previously reached callers through Load's second return value (src/store.go:12 return v, nil / src/store.go:10 return "", ErrMissing) is now unreachable at the call site. Because LoadOrDefault is exported, the degenerate API contract is the defect regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: TTL check inverted: returns expired entries, evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was changed from `< this.ttlMs` to `> this.ttlMs`. `Date.now() - entry.storedAt` is the entry's AGE; it is < ttl when the entry is still fresh. The new condition is true only when the entry is EXPIRED, yet that branch returns entry.value, and the fresh branch below (`this.entries.delete(key); return null`) discards and clears still-valid entries. Net effect: every get() returns stale/expired values while fresh values are deleted and reported as a miss — the cache's entire TTL contract is inverted.

findings.title: pruneDone skips consecutive done jobs and mutates caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: splice(index,1) shifts subsequent elements left while forEach keeps advancing its index, so any done job immediately following a spliced done job is never evaluated and survives. Substitute real values: [{a,done:true},{b,done:true},{c,done:false}] -> index0 splices a -> [{b,true},{c,false}]; index1 now points at c (done:false) and is skipped, leaving b (a done job) in the result. The old filter() also returned a NEW array; this version returns the same array it mutated, so callers holding the original reference now see their data modified in place.

findings.title: TtlCache.get inverted: returns expired entries, deletes fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was flipped from `<` to `>`. Now `get` returns `entry.value` only when `Date.now() - entry.storedAt > this.ttlMs` (entry is EXPIRED), and falls through to `this.entries.delete(key); return null` when the entry is still fresh. Every caller receives stale/expired values as if valid and loses still-valid entries, inverting the entire cache contract.

findings.title: pruneDone skips consecutive done jobs (splice during forEach) and mutates input
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing elements with `jobs.splice(index, 1)` while `forEach` advances the index shifts the following element into the current position, so it is never visited. For `[{done:true},{done:true}]` only the first is removed and the second survives, so pruneDone no longer removes all done jobs. The old `filter` returned a new array; the new body also mutates the caller's array in place, a silent behavior change for callers still holding the reference.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check returns expired cache values and drops fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: `entry.storedAt` is set to `Date.now()` on set (src/cache.ts:12), so age = Date.now() - storedAt is small for fresh entries. The old guard `< this.ttlMs` returned the value while still valid and evicted once expired. Flipping to `>` inverts the semantics: a fresh entry (age < ttl) now falls through to `this.entries.delete(key); return null` while an expired entry (age > ttl) returns its stale value. Every read of a live TTL cache is now wrong in both directions.

findings.title: pruneDone skips done jobs and mutates the caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: Two defects on the same changed lines. (1) `splice` inside `forEach` shifts the array while iteration keeps increasing the index, so an element immediately following a removed done job is skipped and left in the result (e.g. [done, done, not-done] -> first splice removes index 0, then index 1 is skipped, leaving a done job). (2) The previous `jobs.filter(...)` returned a new array; the new body splices `jobs` in place and returns the same reference, so callers now observe their own array silently mutated with done jobs deleted.

findings.title: Bundle.baseSha set to raw base tip, not merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha (line 138) is the PR base branch tip (PR_BASE_SHA = github.event.pull_request.base.sha / gh baseRefOid), which is normally NOT an ancestor of headSha once the base branch advances. mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha) (line 139) is the correct diff base, and it is still used to build bundle.patch and bundle.changedFiles (lines 140-141). Emitting `baseSha` here instead makes the bundle internally inconsistent: the reported base SHA no longer corresponds to the patch/changed-files range. Downstream, review(bundle) (line 177) injects bundle.baseSha as the {{BASE}} used for base-relative git inspection and echoes it as the result's baseSha; substituting the raw tip makes those base..head operations span unrelated base-branch commits (including reversals of changes merged to base after the fork), so the reviewed scope/anchors are wrong whenever base != merge-base.

findings.title: git() maxBuffer removed; >1 MiB patches now fail
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer drops git() to Node's spawnSync default of 1 MiB. git() is used for the full patch (`git diff mergeBase headSha`, line 140). For any PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB (large lockfiles, generated files, many files), spawnSync sets res.error=ENOBUFS and res.status=null, so the check at line 38 (`res.status !== 0`) throws and runGithub falls into its catch, posting a failing check instead of a review. Previously the 64 MiB buffer (matching the adjacent gh/ghText calls at lines 19 and 29) allowed these PRs to be reviewed.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer in git() wrapper (now reverted to 1MB default)
findings.whyItBreaks: The explicit 64MB maxBuffer was deleted, so spawnSync falls back to Node's 1MB default. git() is used for the full PR patch (git diff mergeBase headSha, line 140) and the changed-file list (git diff --name-only, line 57). When output exceeds 1MB, spawnSync returns status=null with error.code=ENOBUFS, so the `res.status !== 0` guard at line 38 throws, runGithub's catch posts a 'Needlefish: review failed' check and exits 1. Large PRs (lockfiles, generated or vendored files) that previously reviewed now hard-fail.

findings.title: Bundle baseSha no longer matches the reviewed diff range
findings.whyItBreaks: The bundle still ships patch = git diff mergeBase headSha (line 140) and changedFiles computed from mergeBase (line 141), where mergeBase = git merge-base baseSha headSha (line 139). But bundle.baseSha is now the live PR base tip (process.env.PR_BASE_SHA, line 138), not mergeBase. Whenever the base branch has advanced past the fork point (baseSha != mergeBase), bundle.baseSha..headSha is a wider range that includes unrelated base-branch commits. Any consumer that re-diffs from bundle.baseSha, or fetches base-side content at bundle.baseSha, inspects a different changeset than the one that was actually reviewed and mis-scopes the review.

findings.title: Dropping git() maxBuffer aborts reviews of large patches
findings.whyItBreaks: git() backs the full patch (spawnSync("git", ["diff", mergeBase, headSha])) as well as --name-only output. Removing maxBuffer drops the 64 MiB cap to Node's spawnSync default of 1024*1024 bytes. A PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated/vendored code) makes spawnSync terminate with ENOBUFS, leaving status null; the `res.status !== 0` check then throws `git diff ... failed: ` (stderr is empty), and because these git calls run before the try/catch in runGithub (lines 139-141 vs 176), the review aborts with no check-run posted.

findings.title: Lenient candidate parse silently drops malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, strict) defaults strict=true, where any finding that fails validation (invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, bad lineStart/lineEnd, blocking severity with confidence<0.7) throws and aborts the review loudly. With strict=false it instead maps each invalid finding to null and filters it out. The candidate pass is the ONLY place original model findings enter the pipeline (critic receives JSON.stringify(candidate) at lines 34-36) and final findings come from pruned.findings (line 48), so a genuinely reported P1/P2 finding that trips one validation rule is removed before the critic can preserve it and never appears in the result. The guard at line 30 only checks summary/checked, so a review with a silently emptied findings list still passes and can ship a false PASS.

findings.title: Candidate pass parsed leniently, silently dropping malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, strict) defaults to strict=true; passing false makes it catch normalizeFinding errors and filter out the offending finding instead of throwing. So a genuine P1/P2 finding emitted by the first (candidate) Codex pass that has one malformed required field (e.g. missing/blank file, severity, lineStart/lineEnd) is silently removed from candidate.findings. The usability guard at line 30 only checks summary and checked.length, not findings, so it does not catch this; the critic call at lines 34-38 is prune-only and receives the already-truncated candidate, and deriveVerdict at line 43 acts on pruned.findings. The dropped finding is unrecoverable, so a PR that should be flagged can yield pass/needs_human. Note the asymmetry: the critic pass at line 38 still uses the strict default, so only the candidate parse was loosened.

findings.title: Do not parse candidate findings non-strictly; drops real findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) is strict by default: it maps findings through the throwing normalizeFinding (throws on invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or lineStart/lineEnd <= 0), so malformed model output previously aborted the review loudly. Passing false takes the non-strict branch, which wraps each finding in try/catch and filters out nulls — a genuinely emitted P0/P1/P2 finding with a single bad field is silently removed from candidate.findings. Those findings are the only input to the critic at line 35, and the critic prunes rather than recovers, so the finding never reaches pruned.findings. deriveVerdict (line 43) returns changes_requested only when a P0/P1/P2 survives, so the dropped finding yields pass. The guard at line 30 does not catch this: summary and checked are still populated when all findings are dropped, so no error is raised. This converts a loud failure into a silent wrong PASS on the merge gate, which is the tool's core function.

findings.title: Explicit 0 duration now silently replaced by the fallback delay
findings.whyItBreaks: Base accepted any finite value >= 0 (`parsed >= 0`), so an operator could set NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 / NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 to escalate/finish immediately (setTimeout(fn, 0) is a valid immediate delay). The new guard `parsed > 0` rejects exactly `"0"` and returns fallbackMs, so those explicit settings now silently become 5000 ms @src/shared/runner-process.ts:124 and 2000 ms @src/shared/runner-process.ts:123 — an upgrade silently overrides an existing configuration value and delays SIGKILL escalation and give-up, with no comment, doc, or test justifying the change.

findings.title: Rejecting 0 silently overrides zero-grace runner config
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`. Substituting "0": `Number.isFinite(0) && 0 > 0` is false, so readRunnerDurationMs returns fallbackMs instead of 0. Its two call sites feed env config: line 3-6 reads NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS (fallback 5000) and line 7-10 reads NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS (fallback 2000). Those constants are used directly as delays: setTimeout(..., RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS) at line 123 and setTimeout(..., RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS) at line 124. Before this change, an operator setting either variable to "0" got the intended 0ms (SIGTERM→SIGKILL immediately, or give up on `close` immediately). After this change that explicit, previously-valid value is silently discarded and replaced by 5s/2s, so the kill/give-up escalation is delayed by seconds with no error or warning — a behavior regression on a live, user-controlled config path.
